title: Cheng-Han Yang
text:
Biostatistics · Yale School of Public Health


Cheng-Han Yang


Associate Research Scientist, Department of Biostatistics · Yale University


I build statistical methods that let electronic health records tell the truth about who seeks care and what gets measured.


Email CV (PDF) Google Scholar GitHub ORCID








                    









About

I am an Associate Research Scientist in the Department of Biostatistics at the Yale School of Public Health, working with Dr. Bhramar Mukherjee. My research develops semiparametric and causal methods for large-scale electronic health records (EHR), where the times a patient is seen, and the moments a biomarker is recorded, are themselves informative about health.


I received my Ph.D. in Biostatistics from UTHealth Houston in 2025, advised by Dr. Ruitao Lin, with a thesis on Bayesian adaptive designs for early-phase oncology trials. My work spans two connected programs: modeling informative visit and observation processes in EHR, and adaptive dose-finding for modern cancer therapeutics.


Research focus



Informative presence & observation in EHR


Semiparametric joint models that correct the biases arising when clinical contact and measurement depend on a patient’s underlying condition.




Adaptive dose-finding design


Seamless phase I–II designs that use biological mediators and survival endpoints to optimize dose for targeted therapies and immunotherapies.




Causal inference from observational data


Estimands and estimators for treatment effects under irregular follow-up, including dynamic regimes in real-world cohorts.




Variable screening & treatment regimes


Model-free screening for high-dimensional survival data that stays valid without assuming an outcome model or a form for the regime.

title: Software
text:
DEMOdesign
Dose Exploration, Monitoring, and Optimization Using Biological and Clinical Outcomes
An R package implementing the DEMO design—a Bayesian adaptive Phase I/II trial framework tailored for oncology dose-finding, particularly for immunotherapies and targeted therapies. It selects an Optimal Therapeutic Dose (OTD) that maximizes Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) while ensuring safety, biological activity, and clinical efficacy across three stages.

Features

Three-stage Bayesian adaptive design (Exploration, Monitoring, Optimization)
Integrates biomarker, toxicity, response, and survival endpoints
BOIN-based exploration with biomarker and toxicity screening
RMST-based dose optimization



Installation
remotes::install_github("cyang728/DEMOdesign")


Reference
Yang CH, Thall PF, Lin R. (2025). “Dose exploration, monitoring, and optimization using biological and clinical outcomes.” Annals of Applied Statistics, 19(4), 2599–2617.
GitHub Repository

title: Software
text:
BAR12
Bayesian Autoregressive Phase 1-2 Design for Cell Therapy Trials with Manufacturing Changes
An R package implementing the BAR12 design for seamless dose-finding in early-phase cell therapy trials that incorporate mid-trial manufacturing modifications—or tweaks—such as changes to cell culture duration, cytokine cocktails, or donor criteria. BAR12 uses a Bayesian autoregressive model with spike-and-slab priors to distinguish between pre- and post-tweak outcome distributions, allowing dynamic borrowing of information while accounting for possible shifts.

Features

Handles mid-trial manufacturing process changes
Bayesian autoregressive model with spike-and-slab priors
Dynamic information borrowing across trial stages
Stan-based posterior computation



Installation
remotes::install_github("cyang728/BAR12")
GitHub Repository

title: Software
text:
MCPModX
Covariate-Adjusted MCP-Mod for Dose-Response Analysis
An R package that incorporates covariate adjustment to enhance the robustness and precision of dose-response analyses. The approach leverages g-computation to address non-collapsibility and employs model-assisted estimation to ensure valid inferences, even in the presence of model misspecification.

Features

Covariate adjustment in MCP-Mod framework
G-computation for non-collapsible endpoints
Support for binary endpoints with prognostic scores
Model-assisted estimation for robust inference



Installation
remotes::install_github("cyang728/MCPModX")

title: Research
text:
My research develops statistical methodology for clinical trials and healthcare data, organized around four connected themes.

Research area

EHR Data Analysis
My current research at Yale focuses on developing statistical methods for analyzing large-scale electronic health records (EHR) data.

Informative Presence (IP) arises when the process governing the availability of patient data, i.e., whether patients are present or absent, is related to the patient’s health condition.
Informative Observation (IO), conditional on a visit, the decision to measure and record an outcome is not random; it may be driven by the patient’s underlying condition or clinical decision-making, rendering the observation indicator informative.

I develop methods that properly account for these clinically informed biases to enable correct estimation of associations from EHR data.



Research area

Adaptive Dose-Finding Design
A central challenge in oncology drug development is identifying the optimal dose that balances safety and efficacy. Traditional phase I designs focus solely on toxicity, but for modern targeted therapies and immunotherapies, higher doses do not always lead to better outcomes.

DEMO: Dose Exploration, Monitoring, and Optimization
The DEMO design is a seamless three-stage adaptive trial design that extends conventional phase I-II designs by incorporating:

Biological endpoints (e.g., PK/PD markers, BCMA levels) as mediators between dose and clinical outcomes
Multiple clinical outcomes: early toxicity, tumor response, and long-term survival
Restricted mean survival time (RMST) as the optimization criterion

The three stages are: (1) sequential dose exploration with elimination of unsafe or biologically inactive doses, (2) randomized dose screening, and (3) randomized dose optimization based on survival outcomes.


Yang C-H, Thall PF, Lin R. (2025). DEMO: Dose exploration, monitoring, and optimization using biological and clinical outcomes. Annals of Applied Statistics, 19(4), 2599–2617. [Paper] [Code]




Conservativeness of BLRM Designs
The Bayesian logistic regression method (BLRM) is widely adopted for finding the MTD in phase I oncology trials. This work examines the relative conservativeness of the standard BLRM design and proposes a dose-switching rule to enhance performance while maintaining safety.


Yang C-H, Cheng G, Lin R. (2024). On the relative conservativeness of Bayesian logistic regression method in oncology dose-finding studies. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 23(4), 585–594. [Paper]






Research area

Clinical Trial Analysis
Single small-sample trials often lack the power to reliably identify the optimal dose. My research develops meta-analytic and modeling approaches to synthesize evidence across multiple studies.

REDOMA: Random-Effects Dose-Optimization Meta-Analysis
The REDOMA method synthesizes toxicity and efficacy data from multiple phase I/II trials to identify the optimal biological dose:

Gamma process prior for curve-free modeling of dose-toxicity relationships
Spike-and-slab prior for automatic variable selection, allowing plateau or non-monotonic dose-efficacy curves
Random-effects framework to account for between-study heterogeneity



Yang C-H, Kwiatkowski E, Lee JJ, Lin R. (2024). REDOMA: Bayesian random-effects dose-optimization meta-analysis using spike-and-slab priors. Statistics in Medicine, 43(18), 3484–3502. [Paper]




MCPModX: Covariate-Adjusted MCP-Mod
MCPModX incorporates covariate adjustment to enhance the robustness and precision of dose-response analyses within the MCP-Mod framework. The MCP-Mod method, qualified by EMA (2014) and FDA (2016) as an efficient statistical method for Phase II dose-finding studies, combines hypothesis testing and dose-response modeling to identify the minimum effective dose under model uncertainty. MCPModX provides:

G-computation for addressing non-collapsibility in binary endpoints
Model-assisted estimation for valid inferences even under model misspecification
Prognostic score adjustment for improved precision



Yang C-H. MCPModX: Covariate-adjusted MCP-Mod for dose-response analysis. [GitHub]






Research area

Optimal Treatment Regime
In precision medicine, treatment decisions should account for the heterogeneity of treatment effects across patients. An optimal treatment regime is a decision rule that assigns treatments to patients based on their individual characteristics to optimize expected clinical outcomes.

Model-Free Variable Screening for Optimal Treatment Regimes
I developed a model-free variable screening method for identifying the optimal treatment regime with high-dimensional survival data. The key innovations include:

Outcome-dependent sampling framework — Reformulating the weighted classification problem into a classification problem within a hypothetical population, where observed data can be viewed as a sample obtained from outcome-dependent sampling
Weighted Kolmogorov–Smirnov approach — Extending the conventional Kolmogorov–Smirnov method for binary classification to select active variables in the optimal treatment regime
Two levels of robustness — (1) No model assumptions required for the survival outcome on treatment and covariates, and (2) the form of treatment regimes can be unspecified without requiring convex surrogate loss
Subgroup-specific analysis — The method can be applied to any prespecified subgroup of the target population, including the treated group as a special case

The proposed screening method is robust to model misspecifications, allowing nonparametric learning methods such as random forests and boosting to be applied to the selected variables for further analysis.


Yang C-H, Cheng Y-J. (2024). A model-free variable screening method for optimal treatment regimes with high-dimensional survival data. Biometrika, 111(4), 1369–1386. [Paper]

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
text: Survival analysis is a branch of statistics that deals with analyzing the time until an event of interest occurs. The Kaplan-Meier (KM) estimator is one of the most fundamental and widely used tools in this field. In this post, I’ll walk through the motivation, mathematics, and intuition behind this elegant method.

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
text: Survival analysis is a branch of statistics that deals with analyzing the time until an event of interest occurs. The Kaplan-Meier (KM) estimator is one of the most fundamental and widely used tools in this field. In this post, I’ll walk through the motivation, mathematics, and intuition behind this elegant method.

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
text:
The Challenge: Censored Data
Our goal is to estimate the survival function: \[
S(t) = P(T > t)
\] which tracks the probability of remaining event-free over time.
The main difficulty arises from right-censoring: we often lose track of subjects before they experience the event (e.g., due to study termination or withdrawal).






Censoring is Information, Not Failure



A censored observation is not a failure. It provides the invaluable information that the subject survived at least until their censoring time. Methods that simply ignore this partial information will incorrectly bias survival estimates downward.


Therefore, a valid method must use information from both events and censored observations.

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
section: The Flaw in the Naive Approach
text:
The Flaw in the Naive Approach
Consider a survival dataset with times in months: \[
6,\ 7,\ 9^+,\ 10,\ 12^+,\ 15 \quad(\text{+ indicates censoring})
\]

A Naive Calculation
What’s the survival probability past 11 months, \(S(11)\)? A simple empirical proportion would be: \[
\widehat{S}_{\text{naive}}(11) = \frac{\text{Number of subjects observed beyond 11 months}}{\text{Total number of subjects}} = \frac{2}{6} \approx 0.333
\] (This only counts the subjects at times \(12^+\) and \(15\).)






Problem



This is wrong because it mishandles censored data. The subject censored at 9 months is known to have survived for at least 9 months. This naive method effectively treats them as if they failed to survive past 11 months, which is incorrect.

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
text:
Notation
For subject \(i = 1, \dots, n\):

\(T_i\): true event time (possibly unobserved)
\(C_i\): censoring time
\(Y_i = \min(T_i, C_i)\): observed time
\(\delta_i = \mathbf{1}(T_i \le C_i)\): event indicator

Let \(t_{(1)} < \cdots < t_{(J)}\) be the distinct event times. At each \(t_{(j)}\):

\(n_j = \#\{\text{at risk just before } t_{(j)}\}\)
\(d_j = \#\{\text{events at } t_{(j)}\} = \#\{i: \delta_i = 1, Y_i = t_{(j)}\}\)
\(c_j = \#\{\text{censored during the interval } [t_{(j)}, t_{(j+1)})\}\)

We take \(S(t) = \Pr(T > t)\) (right-continuous) and \(S(t^-) = \Pr(T \ge t)\) (left limit).

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
text:
The Kaplan-Meier Estimator






Definition



Assuming noninformative censoring (\(T \perp C\)), the survival function can be estimated by: \[
\boxed{\widehat{S}(t) = \prod_{j: t_{(j)} \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)}
\]



Key Properties

The KM estimator drops only at event times
Censored observations reduce later risk sets but do not cause drops
It produces a characteristic step-function plot
The most critical assumption is noninformative censoring
The curve’s precision decreases as the number of subjects at risk diminishes over time

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
section: Mathematical Derivation: KM as Nonparametric MLE
text:
Mathematical Derivation: KM as Nonparametric MLE

The Likelihood Function
Assuming independent censoring (\(T \perp C\)), the likelihood for each subject is:
\[
L(S \mid \text{Data}) \propto \prod_{i=1}^n P(T = t_i)^{\delta_i} P(T_i > t)^{1-\delta_i}
\]
This can be rewritten as: \[
L(S \mid \text{Data}) = \prod_{i=1}^n \{S(t_i^-) - S(t_i)\}^{\delta_i} S(t_i)^{1-\delta_i}
\]
Since all failure mass concentrates on the observed event times \(\{t_{(j)}\}_{j=1}^J\), grouping by event times gives:
\[
\boxed{L(S \mid \text{Data}) \propto \prod_{j=1}^J \big\{S(t_{(j)}^-) - S(t_{(j)})\big\}^{d_j} \times S(t_{(j)})^{c_j}}
\]


Jump and Survival Ratio
At each \(t_{(j)}\), define the jump: \[
\Delta S_j := S(t_{(j)}^-) - S(t_{(j)})
\]
For a subject at risk at \(t_{(j)}\) (i.e., \(T \ge t_{(j)}\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\text{fail at } t_{(j)} \mid \text{at risk at } t_{(j)}) &= \frac{\Delta S_j}{S(t_{(j)}^-)} = \lambda_j \\
\Pr(\text{survive past } t_{(j)} \mid \text{at risk at } t_{(j)}) &= \frac{S(t_{(j)})}{S(t_{(j)}^-)} = 1 - \lambda_j
\end{aligned}
\]


The Key Ratio Identity
For each \(j\): \[
S(t_{(j)}) = (1 - \lambda_j) S(t_{(j)}^-)
\]
Reason: “At risk at \(t_{(j)}\) and not failing at \(t_{(j)}\)” is exactly “surviving to the next event time \(t_{(j+1)}\)”.


Recursion and Telescoping
Rearranging gives: \[
\Pr(T \ge t_{(j+1)}) = \Pr(T \ge t_{(j)})(1 - \lambda_j)
\]
Iterating for \(l = 1, \ldots, j\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(t_{(j)}^-) &= \Pr(T \ge t_{(j)}) = \Pr(T \ge t_{(1)}) \prod_{l=1}^{j-1}(1 - \lambda_l) \\
S(t_{(j)}) &= \Pr(T > t_{(j)}) = \Pr(T \ge t_{(1)}) \prod_{l=1}^j (1 - \lambda_l)
\end{aligned}
\]


Product-Limit Form
Without left truncation, \(\Pr(T \ge t_{(1)}) = 1\). If \(t_{(j)} \le t < t_{(j+1)}\):
\[
\boxed{S(t) = \Pr(T > t) = \prod_{t_{(j)} \le t}(1 - \lambda_j)}
\]


Maximizing the Likelihood
The likelihood can be rewritten as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(S \mid \text{Data}) &\propto \prod_{j=1}^J \big\{S(t_{(j)}^-) - S(t_{(j)})\big\}^{d_j} \times S(t_{(j)})^{c_j} \\
&= \prod_{j=1}^J \lambda_j^{d_j} \prod_{k=1}^{j-1} (1-\lambda_k)^{d_j} \times \prod_{k=1}^j (1-\lambda_k)^{c_j} \\
&= \prod_{j=1}^J \lambda_j^{d_j} (1-\lambda_j)^{n_j - d_j}
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the log-likelihood for each \(\lambda_j\): \[
\ell_j(\lambda_j) = d_j \log \lambda_j + (n_j - d_j) \log(1 - \lambda_j)
\]
Setting the derivative to zero: \[
\boxed{\widehat{\lambda}_j = \frac{d_j}{n_j}}
\]
Therefore: \[
\widehat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_{(j)} \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)
\]
This is the Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) estimator, and we have shown it is the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator for the survival function under independent censoring.

title: Survival Analysis: Understanding the Kaplan-Meier Estimator
text:
Summary
The Kaplan-Meier estimator is:

Intuitive: It multiplies conditional survival probabilities at each event time
Principled: It is the nonparametric MLE under independent censoring
Practical: It correctly handles censored observations
Visual: The step-function plot provides an immediate understanding of survival patterns

Understanding the KM estimator is essential for anyone working with time-to-event data in clinical trials, reliability engineering, or any field where survival analysis is applied.
